title: The Synagogue Repents and the Bride Is Praised
english: So this is the voice of the repentant Synagogue speaking to Christ: 'Make Yourself known to me, so that, while You shepherd the Churches of Your companions, I may not remain with the veil over my heart' (Song of Songs 1:7). 'If you do not know yourself' (Song of Songs 1:8): that is, 'If you do not repent,' He says, 'you will be found behind the nations, since you have no fruits of righteousness but remain fruitless, and behind the flocks that I have gathered to Myself.'

'I have likened you to My mare' (Song of Songs 1:9): that is, 'Having received My faith, O Church, you have been likened to the apostles.' Of them it is said, 'You will mount upon Your horses, and Your riding is salvation' (Habakkuk 3:8); and they were made ready against the chariots of the unseen Pharaoh. 'Your cheeks are like a turtledove's' (Song of Songs 1:10): through the turtledove He shows her modesty toward the Bridegroom, for the turtledove's cheeks are red.

To the Synagogue, on the contrary, it is said: 'You had the face of a prostitute; you were shameless toward all' (Jeremiah 3:3). By the neck (Song of Songs 1:10) He means the soul's readiness to submit; for what a fine ornament is a neck that has learned to bear the yoke of Christ (Matthew 11:29)! In Scripture, silver usually stands for divine teaching, and gold for divine gifts (Song of Songs 1:11). Before Christ came among us, all things were likenesses and, as the Apostle says, a shadow of the good things to come (Hebrews 10:1). But Christ, having risen, has given humankind what is perfect; before the resurrection we had likenesses, drawn from the praises of Him in the Law and the Prophets.

The nard and the bundle of myrrh (Song of Songs 1:12–13) signify the burial of Christ: Nicodemus brought these and wrapped His body in them (John 19:39–40). For breasts the bride has the two Testaments, and between them Christ lodges (Song of Songs 1:13).

The Bridegroom calls her beautiful, no longer only 'among women' as before (Song of Songs 1:8), but now also as one near Him, and so He doubles His praise of the bride (Song of Songs 1:15), praising both her contemplation and her action. By eyes He means the eyes of the mind and heart; and 'of a dove' marks their clear sight, in the sense in which the dove is also taken for the Spirit. He says, then, that the bride has received a mind that sees God alone.
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum canticorum (Greek). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.

In the Greek the opening words 'Φωνὴ οὖν, ἡ' stand at the end of the previous section and the closing words 'μόνον ὁρῶντα Θεόν' at the start of the next; both are translated here so the sentences are whole.
'ὅπως μὴ [cod. μοι]' follows the editor's μή: the Synagogue asks that she may not remain veiled.
'παρὰ τῶν ἐπαίνων [ita cod.] αὐτοῦ' is kept as 'the praises of Him'.
'νοητοῦ Φαραώ' is rendered 'unseen Pharaoh'.
The garbled 'περιστερᾶς τὸ διορατικοὺς' is rendered by sense ('of a dove' marks clear sight).
The stray '1' inside the Greek of this section is a print number and is not translated.
baehrens: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum u01 rem early

title: The Lily of the Valleys and the Archer
english: The eyes are also the Church's teachers, guileless and keen-sighted. 'I am a flower of the plain, a lily of the valleys' (Song of Songs 2:1). Since the bride has received the rain from above and has borne virtue, she compares herself to a flower of the plain; and she shows how much the coming of Christ has helped, since it has shown even the valleys, unfit for any sowing, full of such flowers. For by a valley she means what the demons who once dwelt in it had hollowed out.

'Hem me in with apples' (Song of Songs 2:5): make me safe with the words of the Gospel, for these breathe the fragrance of Christ upon us. 'And may I too,' she says, 'be ranked with His saints'; for as He is an apple tree (Song of Songs 2:3), so those who share His body and partake with Him (Ephesians 3:6) are apples.

'His left hand…' (Song of Songs 2:6). The left hand is the Law, the right the Gospel. Or else the left is the present life and the right the life to come: the right hand that will embrace me when He says to those on His right, 'Come, you blessed of My Father' (Matthew 25:34). It also says elsewhere, 'Length of life and years of life are in the right hand of Wisdom, and in her left are riches and glory' (Proverbs 3:16). Her right hand, then, is the knowledge of divine things, from which comes eternal life; her left is the knowledge of human things, from which come riches and glory. So she says, 'My mind rises above human things, and divine knowledge will cover me.' For it is said again, 'Honor her, that she may embrace you' (Proverbs 4:8).

This shows, then, that the same One is both our Bridegroom and our Archer, and that the purified soul is both bride and arrow. As an arrow, then, He aims her at the good mark; as a bride He takes her up into fellowship in incorruptible eternity, granting through the right hand length of life and years of life (Proverbs 3:16), and through the left the riches of eternal goods and the glory of God, in which those who seek the glory of the world have no share. That is why she says, 'His left hand is at my head' (Song of Songs 2:6), the hand by which the arrow is aimed at the mark.
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum canticorum (Greek). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.
The opening Greek words 'μόνον ὁρῶντα Θεόν' are translated at the end of the previous section.
εὐώνυμος means 'left' (the left hand of Song of Songs 2:6).
The phrase 'ἐν δεξιᾷ τῆς σοφίας' (Proverbs 3:16) is given in natural English word order.
The closing clause 'εὐθύνεται ὑπὸ τὸν σκοπὸν τὸ βέλος' stands at the head of the next section in the Greek and is translated here so the sentence is whole.
The source reads 'ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλήν' where the LXX has ὑπό, so it is rendered 'at my head', which fits both the archery reading here and the pillow reading in the next section.
baehrens: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum u01 rem mid

title: The Embrace of the Right Hand
english: And His right hand, taking hold of me and drawing me toward Himself, makes me light for the upward flight; so that, sent there and yet not parted from the Archer, I rather come to rest.

Then she turns her words to the daughters of the Jerusalem above (Song of Songs 2:7; Galatians 4:26). Her words are an appeal, made under oath, to make love abound and grow ever greater, until He who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4) brings His will to fulfillment.

By the left hand, it seems, she hints at the good things of the present life, which she already enjoys; by the right, at the expectation of the things to come, held in promises. Their use, she says, as has been said, lies in promises and hopes. And it is well said that she is embraced by the right hand and that her head rests on the left. For the things of the present life, however useful and admired they may be thought, must be placed beneath the head of the perfect soul, supplying the body only with what it needs, as a pillow does for the head. But the things of the age to come, since they are divine and stand above human nature, she hinted at as surpassing by speaking of the embrace.

Or perhaps, since hands are a symbol of actions, the actions of the left hand signify what belongs to the body and those of the right what belongs to the soul; and these, being on the right, have received the better lot and hold the needs of the body in their embrace. For as the embracing hand is above and holds within its arm what it embraces, so the actions directed toward the goal of the life to come hold fast every irrational movement of the body and keep life well ordered and bound together; and no one is able to plot against the soul that the Bridegroom has embraced.
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum canticorum (Greek). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.
The opening Greek clause 'εὐθύνεται ὑπὸ τὸν σκοπὸν τὸ βέλος' is translated at the end of the previous section.
'τοῦ τοξότου' is rendered 'the Archer', capitalized because it means Christ.
παράκλησις here means an appeal: the bride binds the daughters of Jerusalem by an oath (Song of Songs 2:7).
προσκεφάλαιον is a pillow.
The garbled 'περιέχονται' is rendered by sense as active ('hold … in their embrace').
The stray '2' at the end of the Greek section is a print number and is not translated.
baehrens: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum u01 rem close
